parts.label: (a)
hints: Hint 1: Start by thinking about the type of nucleus involved - is it stable or unstable, and can anything outside trigger or stop what happens to it?
Hint 2: Think about what leaves the nucleus when it changes - what kind of particles or radiation are emitted in this spontaneous process?
parts.proper_answer: Spontaneous disintegration of an unstable nucleus with emission of alpha, beta or gamma radiation.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What Is Actually Decaying**
Think of a nucleus that has too many neutrons or protons to stay together comfortably. It is unstable, so sooner or later it will rearrange itself into a more stable form. That change of the nucleus itself is what we call decay.

Step 2: **Why Spontaneous Matters**
Spontaneous means it happens on its own, randomly and without any outside trigger. You cannot make it happen faster by heating, cooling or applying pressure. Each unstable nucleus has a fixed probability of decaying per unit time, but you cannot predict when a particular one will go.

Step 3: **Putting The Full Definition Together**
When the unstable nucleus breaks up it ejects energy and mass as ionising radiation. So in one compact sentence: $$ \text{radioactive decay = spontaneous disintegration of an unstable nucleus with emission of radiation} $$ That covers both marking ideas: unstable nucleus emitting radiation, and the process being spontaneous.

parts.label: (b)(i)
key_concepts: decay constant and A = lambda N
hints: Hint 1: Remember what activity means on an $N$ against $t$ graph - it is the rate at which $N$ is falling, so how could you get it from the shape of the curve or from $N$ itself?
Hint 2: Look at the starting value $N_0$ at $t = 0$ on Fig. 13.1 and find the time taken for $N$ to fall to half that value - what does that time tell you?
Hint 3: That half-life time must be in seconds for SI units, so convert minutes to seconds and think how $\lambda$ is linked to half-life by $\ln 2$.
Hint 4: Read the value of $N$ at $t = 14.0$ minutes from the graph and combine it with $\lambda$ using $A = \lambda N$ to get activity in $\text{Bq}$.
parts.proper_answer: Half-life $T_{1/2} \approx 14$ min, $N = 4.4 \times 10^7$ at $t = 14.0$ min, $A = \lambda N = 3.6 \times 10^4\text{ Bq}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Two Ways To Get Activity From The Graph**
Activity is the decay rate: $$ A = -\frac{\Delta N}{\Delta t} = \lambda N $$ So you can either draw a tangent at $t = 14.0$ min and find its gradient magnitude, or find the half-life and use $A = \lambda N$. The half-life route is neater here because $t = 14.0$ min is very close to one half-life.

Step 2: **Read The Half-Life From Fig. 13.1**
At $t = 0$, $N_0 \approx 8.8 \times 10^7$. Half of this is: $$ \frac{N_0}{2} \approx 4.4 \times 10^7 $$ Find $4.4 \times 10^7$ on the vertical axis and read across to the curve, then down to the time axis. You land at about $t = 14$ min. So: $$ T_{1/2} \approx 14 \text{ min} = 14 \times 60 = 840 \text{ s} $$

Step 3: **Get The Decay Constant**
The link between half-life and decay constant is: $$ \lambda = \frac{\ln 2}{T_{1/2}} $$ Put the time in seconds: $$ \lambda = \frac{0.693}{840} \approx 8.25 \times 10^{-4} \text{ s}^{-1} $$ Always convert to seconds because activity in becquerel means decays per second.

Step 4: **Calculate Activity At 14.0 Minutes**
At $t = 14.0$ min the graph gives: $$ N = 4.4 \times 10^7 $$ Then: $$ A = \lambda N = (8.25 \times 10^{-4})(4.4 \times 10^7) $$ $$ A \approx 3.6 \times 10^4 \text{ Bq} $$ This makes sense - after one half-life the activity is half its initial value, and the unit $\text{Bq}$ is $\text{s}^{-1}$.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
key_concepts: decay constant as probability per unit time
hints: Hint 1: Focus on the direct link between the activity you just found and the number of undecayed nuclei present at that same instant - which simple equation connects $A$, $\lambda$ and $N$?
Hint 2: Read $N$ at $t = 14.0$ minutes from Fig. 13.1 again and rearrange to make $\lambda$ the subject, remembering $A$ must be in $\text{Bq}$ so $\lambda$ comes out in $\text{s}^{-1}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use Activity Directly**
You do not need the half-life formula here. Activity and number of nuclei at the same moment are linked by: $$ A = \lambda N $$ This is true at any instant, so use the values at $t = 14.0$ min.

Step 2: **Substitute And Solve For Lambda**
From (i), $A \approx 3.6 \times 10^4 \text{ Bq}$ and from the graph at $t = 14.0$ min, $N = 4.4 \times 10^7$. Rearranging: $$ \lambda = \frac{A}{N} = \frac{3.6 \times 10^4}{4.4 \times 10^7} $$ $$ \lambda \approx 8.2 \times 10^{-4} \text{ s}^{-1} $$ The small value tells you each nucleus has only a tiny probability of decaying in one second, as expected for a half-life of many minutes.
